en: The Discourse Spoken by the Buddha on the Cause for Guarding Against All Outflows, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kuru, where he gathered the assembly to deliberate upon the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!..."
He replied, “Yes, sir.
The bhikṣu then received the instruction from the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke thus:
"O bhikṣus, for the one who sees with wisdom, the outflows are exhausted;
for the one who lacks wisdom and does not see, the outflows are not exhausted."
"What, monks, is it that for one who is wise and sees, the floods are brought to an end, whereas for one who is unwise and does not see, the floods are not brought to an end?
It is simply a matter of whether one practices the fundamental contemplation or does not practice the fundamental contemplation."
For one who does not practice the fundamental contemplation, where there was no desire, desire arises; once desire has arisen, it increases and does not cease.
Where there was no flow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) nor flow of ignorance (*moha-āsrava*), these arise; once they have arisen, they increase and do not cease.

"O monks! One who is deluded and has not heard—such a person among the worldlings does not see the wise, nor do they hear the Dharma from the wise, nor do they receive instruction and admonition from the wise, nor do they analyze and understand through the wise; thus, they fall into what is contrary to their original mindfulness."

It causes the stream that has not yet arisen to arise, and it causes the stream that has already arisen to increase and flourish; likewise, it causes the existence that has not yet arisen to arise through delusion, and it causes the existence that has already arisen to increase and flourish through delusion.

Because one does not know and does not understand, one contemplates those things that should not be contemplated as if there were an injunction to do so, while failing to contemplate those things that ought to be contemplated.

By not contemplating what should be contemplated and contemplating what should not be contemplated, the flow of craving arises; once the flow of craving has arisen, it increases and expands. Furthermore, the flow of delusion arises where it had not yet arisen, and where the flow of craving and the flow of delusion have already arisen, they increase and expand.

"O monks! A disciple of the Dharma who has heard [the teaching], who possesses insight, and who receives instruction from one possessed of insight, and who likewise analyzes and understands through one possessed of insight—such a person is one who knows according to reality."

For one who lacks right mindfulness, the flow of craving arises when it has not yet arisen, and once arisen, it increases and does not subside; likewise, the flow of delusion arises when it has not yet arisen, and once arisen, it increases and does not subside.

As for fundamental mindfulness: it prevents the unarisen flow of craving from arising, and enables the abandonment of the arisen flow of craving; it likewise prevents the unarisen flow of delusion from arising, and enables the abandonment of the arisen flow of delusion.
If one possesses such knowledge regarding the phenomena that should be attended to, one does not attend to what should not be attended to, but attends to those phenomena that should be attended to.

By not attending to phenomena that should not be attended to and attending to those phenomena that should be attended to, one prevents unarisen taints of craving from arising and abandons and resolves upon those taints of craving already arisen; likewise, one prevents unarisen taints of delusion from arising and abandons and resolves upon those taints of delusion already arisen.
“Furthermore, there are seven kinds of monks who, from this, give rise to affliction, from this, heat, and from this, sorrow.
What are the seven?
There are, monks! [monks who...]”

There are outflows to be abandoned through vision; there are outflows to be abandoned through inclusion; there are outflows to be abandoned through avoidance; there are outflows to be abandoned through further contact; there are outflows to be abandoned through patience; there are outflows to be abandoned through clear comprehension; and there are outflows to be abandoned through the practice of mindfulness.
“What, monks, are the floods that are abandoned through vision?
These, monks, are what is heard.”

Being deluded and not having heard [the Dharma], a person of the world neither sees the noble ones, nor understands from the noble ones, nor understands the instructions and admonitions of the noble ones; thus, they do not reflect upon such fundamental questions as:
"Did I exist in a previous life?"
Did I exist in previous lives?
What was I in previous lives?
How was I in previous lives?
Will I exist in future lives?
Will I not exist in future lives?
What will I become in future lives?
What shall I become in future lives? What doubts do I harbor regarding my own self?
And from where has this person come?
"To where shall I go again?
What must I do about this?
Because one does not maintain such original mindfulness, the six sense bases give rise to doubt and various fetters arise.
Does Zhuangzi have this body?
Does Zhuangzi not have this body?
From this arises doubt, and from doubt arises the self-conceptualization of the body as a "body-view" (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
When such doubt arises, it gives rise to the conceit that "this body is my body";

when such doubt arises, it gives rise to the view of a self in what is merely the body and its characteristics; when such doubt arises, it gives rise to the view of a self where there is no body, taking it to be a body; when such doubt arises, it gives rise to the calculation that "this is my body."

Whatever has been awakened to, whatever has been taught, whatever has been done, whatever has been experienced, whatever has been raised up, and whatever has been initiated—in each and every such place, for whatever good or evil deeds one has performed and whatever retribution one has received, whether they have ceased and do not arise, or whether they both cease and yet arise, it is likewise so.
"Yes, bhikkhus! Fetters cause one to be fettered;
doubt causes one to be doubtful. Evil doubt and wrong view, together with jumping at doubt and the fetter of doubt, become mutually attached, bhikkhus!"
Those who do not hear, O bhikkhus, are the people of the world; from this arises the accumulation of suffering, and from this arises its manifestation.
Those who hear, O bhikkhus, are the disciples of the Way;
they know suffering as it truly is, they know its accumulation as it truly is, they know its cessation as it truly is, and they know the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
Having known thus and seen thus, the three fetters are completely exhausted:
first, the fetter of identity; second, the fetter of doubt; and third, the fetter of attachment to precepts and vows.
Because these three fetters are exhausted, one attains the first fruit in accordance with the Path; one no longer falls into evil states and shall attain deliverance from the world.
Among humans and devas, one will not pass through more than seven lifetimes; having undergone seven lifetimes, one will then bring an end to suffering.

"Monks, the flood that arises for one who does not know and does not see—causing affliction, fever, and sorrow—is severed by one who sees. Because this flood, affliction, fever, and sorrow no longer exist, this, monks, is called [the cessation of the flood]."
"It is through the cessation of views that the outflows are severed. And what, bhikkhu,
is the guarding by which the outflows are severed?"
Monks, when a practitioner who has heard [the Dharma] sees a form with the eye, he restrains the faculty of the eye and maintains self-control,
practicing the contemplation of impurity and reflecting on its original source of birth. Monks!

If the eye-faculty is not guarded and restrained, one practices by contemplating the foul; from this, there flow afflictions, fever, and distress born of mindfulness. By guarding and restraining the eye-faculty, one brings them to cessation; then, through the contemplation of the foul as the fundamental basis, those flowing afflictions, fevers, and distresses no longer exist. This, bhikṣus, is what it means.
The flow ceases through guarding.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"What is it, bhikkhu? [he asked].
How does one flow away from what should be abandoned?

This refers to a practitioner who, having heard [the teaching], ought to practice self-restraint by avoiding vicious elephants, avoiding vicious horses, avoiding vicious oxen, avoiding vicious dogs, avoiding vicious snakes, avoiding deep pits, avoiding thorns, avoiding mountain torrents, avoiding precipices, avoiding ponds and pools, avoiding mountains, avoiding places of insecurity, avoiding rivers, avoiding deep ravines, avoiding evil friends, avoiding evil companions, avoiding evil pursuits, avoiding evil acquisitions, avoiding evil locations, and avoiding evil bedding and seats upon which one lies.
"From the wise, doubt arises; thus it should be, O bhikṣu! You should avoid it.

As explained above, if one does not abandon it, the resulting flow of affliction, fever, and sorrow will arise; having avoided them, one ensures that this flow of affliction, fever, and sorrow shall not exist again. This, O bhikṣu, is called [the practice]."
The outflows are abandoned through avoidance.
"What, monks, is the abandonment of the outflows through utilization?

As for the practitioner who hears this, he uses his robes not for ornament, not for pleasure, not out of greed, and not for adornment; rather, they are used only to ward off mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, sun, and contact with venomous creatures, and to maintain self-restraint when distracted thoughts arise. He takes food not for pleasure, not out of greed, not for strength, and not for physical beauty; rather, it is taken only so that this body may endure to practice the Path and so that [cravings] may be cut off through such sustenance.
Painful sensations and new painful sensations no longer arise; he causes them to subside and does not follow after them.

Having attained strength and dwelling in peace, regarding the bedding, mats, and seats he uses, he does so not for the sake of ornamentation, nor for pleasure, nor out of greed, nor for the sake of adornment, but solely so that this body may be maintained for its necessary function.
It brings rest to those who are weary and exhausted; it allows one to employ what is pleasant and to enjoy what is used for pleasure,
because it is not for ornamentation, not for indulgence, not out of greed, and not for the sake of adornment,
but solely to sever the arising of intense, extreme, and unbearable painful sensations from this very body, and to bring about their cessation.

The cessation of craving: if a bhikṣu, because he does not employ [craving], gives rise to no further flow, affliction, fever, or sorrow, and through employing [the path] brings about its cessation, so that there is no more flow, affliction, fever, or sorrow for him—this, monks, is called [the cessation of craving].
"One attains the further severance of the outflows.
What, bhikṣu, is the severance of the outflows through patience? "

This practitioner who hears [the teaching] as a bhikṣu arouses energetic practice to sever unwholesome dharmas and undertake the practice of pure dharmas; he increases his courage and strength, makes firm his skillful means of diligence, and does not abandon the pure dharma.

By skillful means, he permits this body’s flesh, muscle, bone, marrow, fat, and skin to wither and decay; yet, whatever vigor should be exerted and attained, he ensures that those who possess courage, steadfastness, and the application of vigor do not cease their striving before they have attained what they seek.

The bhikṣu who practices accordingly is able to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, and the sun’s glare; he can bring to rest those things that harbor poison. From the time he has heard improper speech and the conceited mind, he is able to endure and find leisure, thereby overcoming and stilling the painful afflictions born of existence and the intense, disagreeable pains that harbor poison.

If, bhikkhus! one does not allow the flow of fever, vexation, and sorrow born of intolerance to proceed from that fault or from such conduct, but instead brings it to cessation so that they no longer flow as vexation, fever, or sorrow—this, bhikkhus, is called [the end of suffering].
The floods are severed through patience.
"And what, monks, is the severing of the floods through clear comprehension?
It is this, monks: hearing."
When a desire has arisen, a bhikṣu does not tolerate it nor allow it to persist;
he abandons it, understands its characteristics, and distances himself from it.
When anger has arisen, he does not tolerate it nor allow it to persist.
Abandoning, understanding the characteristics, and distancing oneself;

having abandoned, understood the characteristics of, and distanced oneself from killing, deception, and theft that have already arisen, one does not consent to them, does not transgress them, abandons them, understands their characteristics, and distances oneself from them. If, O bhikṣus!

Not following after what has dawned, one does not give rise to the outflows, afflictions, fever, and sorrow; having followed after what has dawned, one does not give rise to them, thereby causing those outflows, afflictions, fever, and sorrow to cease to exist ever again. This, monks, is called... [the cessation of craving].
The floods are severed from the dawn onwards. "What, monks,
is the severing of the floods through the practice of increase?

Having heard this, the monks applied their minds; with their minds awakened, they cultivated increased mindfulness and practice, sitting alone to still themselves, abandon attachment, distance themselves from evil, and turn toward the Dharma.

It was the same for the awakening of discernment (*vīmaṃsā-sambojjhaṅga*), the awakening of energy (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*), the awakening of joy (*pīti-sambojjhaṅga*), the awakening of tranquility (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*), the awakening of concentration (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*), and the awakening of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*); they likewise abandoned heedlessness, transgression, indifference, and the perception of signs.
If, monks, that which has arisen as a flow of affliction, distress, fever,

and sorrow does not increase through non-practice and increases through practice, so that this flow of affliction, distress, fever, and sorrow no longer exists, this, monks, is called [the cessation of suffering].
The floods are abandoned by means of the increase of practice. "Monks,
as for those floods that should be abandoned through vision, they have already been abandoned through vision."
If that which flows forth should be abandoned through guarding and restraint, it has already been abandoned through guarding and restraint;
if the cause of that flow should be abandoned through avoidance, it has already been abandoned through avoidance;
if the cause of that flow should be abandoned through utilization, it has already been abandoned through utilization.
If the cause of the taints is to be abandoned through patience, it has already been abandoned through patience;
if the cause of the taints is to be abandoned through clear knowledge, it has already been abandoned through clear knowledge;
if the cause of the taints is to be abandoned through cultivation, it has already been abandoned through cultivation.
This, O monks, is called the cause for the restraint of all taints;
having destroyed evil craving, one attains transcendence from the world, abandons fetters and bonds, and obtains the essential liberation from suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this, the bhikṣu who heard it received it with joy in his mind and practiced accordingly; he attained liberation from the world and realized the Way.
This is the *Sarvasrotāpattidharanahetuka-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Cause for Guarding Against All Floods) as taught by the Buddha.
